lessons.title: Start here: what is an MRI image?
lessons.blurb: New to MRI? Read this first. What the greys actually mean.

steps.text: This is a single slice through the head, a thin slab of tissue, seen from above. Every pixel is a brightness: how much signal that bit of tissue gave back. Bright = lots of signal, dark = little. MRI doesn't measure 'density' like a CT, it measures how the tissue's water responds to the scan. Nothing to do yet; just look.

Don't know what you're looking at? The labels on this image name the main structures. The big paired blobs deep in the middle are the ventricles, fluid spaces. The outer ribbon is grey matter; the bright bulk inside is white matter.
Every pixel is a tissue with three key numbers, T1, T2 and PD. Those three properties, plus the scan settings, are all that decide how bright the pixel is. The next lessons show how.

lessons.title: Start here: dark or bright? T1 vs T2
lessons.blurb: The one rule that tells the two commonest scans apart.

steps.text: Look at the fluid in the ventricles (centre). Right now it's dark. This is a T1-weighted scan. Fat and white matter are bright, water/fluid is dark. Memory hook: on T1, fluid is dark. (T1 scans look 'anatomical', close to how you'd picture the tissue.)

Two settings have changed here (TR and TE, more on those later), and the ventricles are now bright. This is a T2-weighted scan: fluid is bright. T2 is how you spot disease. Most problems (swelling, fluid, inflammation) light up bright. Memory hook: T2, fluid is bright.

That's the whole trick for reading a scan at a glance: find the fluid (the ventricles, or the eyeballs). Dark fluid → T1. Bright fluid → T2. Flip back and forth with Back / Next until it sticks, it's the single most useful habit in MRI.

lessons.title: Start here: why so many sequences?
lessons.blurb: What 'sequence' means, and why there are dozens of them.

steps.text: A sequence is the recipe of radio pulses and timings the scanner plays. Different recipes make different tissues bright or dark, so radiologists run several per study, each tuned to show something. A plain-language note beneath the image explains what each sequence is for. This is Spin Echo, the reliable all-rounder.

This image switches to FLAIR (an inversion-recovery trick). It's a T2 scan but with the bright fluid switched off. The ventricles go black. Why? So a bright spot sitting next to fluid isn't hidden by it. FLAIR is the workhorse for finding brain lesions. The note beneath the image changes to match.

Last one: Gradient Echo, a fast recipe used for 3-D scans and angiography. The point isn't to memorise them: it's that each sequence is just a different recipe that makes a chosen tissue stand out. When you're ready, the lessons below open up TR, TE, nulling, SNR and FOV planning one at a time.

lessons.title: Start here: spot the lesion (why it matters)
lessons.blurb: The payoff: find a hidden lesion, and see why FLAIR exists.

steps.text: I've added a small lesion to the white matter (choose one any time under Pathology). This is a T1-weighted scan, and the lesion is nearly invisible: its T1 is close to normal white matter, so it barely stands out. Stare at the white matter; you might just make out a faint patch. This is why T1 alone can miss disease.

Now T2-weighted (long TR, long TE). The lesion holds extra water → long T2 → it lights up bright. Suddenly obvious. This is the find-the-fluid rule from the last lesson working for you: pathology usually means extra water, and water is bright on T2.

One problem: bright lesions next to the bright CSF of the ventricles can hide. FLAIR fixes it. It's a T2 scan with the CSF signal switched off, so fluid goes black while the lesion stays bright. That contrast is exactly why FLAIR is run on nearly every brain MRI. The anatomy labels here confirm which bright spot is the lesion.

lessons.title: T1, T2 & PD contrast
lessons.blurb: Why CSF flips from dark to bright as you change TR and TE.

steps.text: T1-weighted. Short TR / short TE on a spin echo. Short-T1 tissues (fat, white matter) recover fast and look bright; fluid (CSF) recovers slowly and stays dark.

T2-weighted. Lengthen TR (drop T1 weighting) and TE (add T2 weighting). Fluid has a long T2, so CSF is now the brightest. The classic flip is clearest in the ventricles, now the brightest structures in the image.
Proton-density. Long TR, short TE, little T1 or T2 weighting, so contrast tracks tissue water content. Gray matter is slightly brighter than white. The 'in-between' weighting.

lessons.title: Nulling a tissue: FLAIR & STIR
lessons.blurb: Inversion recovery and choosing TI to zero out CSF or fat.

steps.text: Inversion recovery flips the magnetization 180°, then waits a time TI before imaging. Each tissue crosses zero signal at TI ≈ T1·ln2. Pick TI to null a tissue.
FLAIR. At 3 T, TI ≈ 2550 ms nulls CSF. Fluid goes dark while T2 contrast remains, so periventricular lesions stand out against black CSF. The workhorse brain sequence.
STIR. Drop TI to ~265 ms and shorten TR. Now fat is nulled instead (short-T1 inversion recovery), used to suppress fat and reveal edema.

lessons.title: SNR vs. scan time
lessons.blurb: The fundamental tradeoff, averaging, matrix, bandwidth.

steps.text: The SNR and scan time readouts on the right show the baseline: one average, 256 matrix.
Averaging (NEX = 4). SNR rises by √4 = 2×, but scan time grows 4×. Averaging buys SNR at a steep time cost.
Resolution. Back to NEX 1, matrix 128: faster and higher SNR per (larger) voxel, but coarser detail. Resolution, SNR and time are always in tension.

lessons.title: Measuring the image: ruler, ROI & SNR
lessons.blurb: Use the on-image tools to read distance, signal and noise.

steps.text: A ruler line is drawn across the image, measuring the width of the ventricles. The readout shows the distance in mm, calibrated to the field of view shown in the corner.

An ROI ellipse sits over white matter, reporting the mean signal and the noise (SD). A second ROI sits over a dark background corner: its mean is ~0 and its SD is the image noise. SNR ≈ tissue mean ÷ background SD.
With NEX raised to 4, the tissue ROI mean holds but the background SD drops, so SNR climbs by √4 = 2× (at 4× the scan time). The ROI readouts make the SNR-time tradeoff visible directly on the image.

lessons.title: When images go wrong: artifacts
lessons.blurb: Motion, chemical shift and dropout, and the setting that fixes each.

steps.text: Motion. The patient moved during the scan, so the image repeats as ghosts along the phase-encode direction. Faint copies of the brain march across the image. The fix: averaging (raise NEX), faster sequences, or a breath-hold.

Chemical shift. Fat and water resonate at slightly different frequencies, so fat is mis-mapped along the readout. A bright and dark edge appears where the fatty scalp meets brain. It worsens at low bandwidth and high field. The fix: raise the receiver bandwidth or use fat-sat.

Susceptibility. Near air and bone (sinuses, ear canals) the field distorts and signal drops out and blooms, worst on gradient echo and at long TE, as seen here. The fix: shorten TE, or use a spin echo instead, since its 180 degree pulse refocuses the dephasing and shrinks the dropout.

lessons.title: 3D slab acquisition & reformat
lessons.blurb: Acquire a slab once, then view any plane.

steps.text: This is a 3D slab acquisition on a gradient echo. The slab is phase-encoded through-plane (kz) and acquired once; note the 3D SLAB badge.
This is the same acquired slab shown in coronal: reformatted from the same acquisition, no re-scan (see the REFORMAT tag). That's the headline of 3D imaging.

And sagittal, still from the one acquisition. The slab readout below shows thin isotropic partitions, the total slab coverage, and a √Nz SNR gain over a single 2D slice, that's what phase-encoding the slice direction buys.
More partitions mean more √Nz signal but a longer scan. Here the partitions have dropped to 16, and the SNR-gain figure falls accordingly (√16 = 4× vs √32 ≈ 5.7×) while the scan time shortens.
With kz partial Fourier turned on, part of the slice-encode k-space is skipped to cut the scan further, trading a little SNR (√PF). The slab still reformats to any plane, the headline of 3D imaging.

lessons.title: Where contrast comes from
lessons.blurb: Read the whole TR×TE landscape, not just one curve.

steps.text: The Contrast map (TR×TE) below the curve shades how strongly two tissues differ across every TR/TE. Bright = high contrast, and the circle marks the current protocol. This is T1-weighted: short TR, short TE.
This is T2-weighted (long TR, long TE). The marker sits in the bright lobe where gray/white matter, and especially CSF, separate most. The picture's contrast follows the map.

Now proton-density (long TR, short TE): GM/WM contrast comes purely from water content. Notice the dark low-contrast band a protocol must avoid. That's where the two tissues' signals cross and the image goes flat.

lessons.title: Multi-slice cross-talk & the gap
lessons.blurb: Why packing slices tight costs SNR, and the gap that fixes it.

steps.text: This is the FOV planning view, showing the SNR readout for one slice, the baseline. The localizer shows a single band of the slice thickness.
Here is a contiguous stack, 16 slices, no gap. The bands fill the slab on the cross panels, but SNR drops: each slice-select pulse saturates the edges of its neighbours (cross-talk).
With a slice gap added (5 mm), the bands separate and the SNR recovers, the classic reason for an inter-slice gap. The trade is coverage vs. signal.

lessons.title: Pathology → the right sequence
lessons.blurb: Why we run DWI, SWI and post-contrast: each catches a different lesion.

steps.text: Under Pathology I've added an acute stroke. It restricts water diffusion, so on DWI (high b-value) it lights up bright while normal brain darkens, the earliest, most sensitive sign of infarction, often positive within minutes. On routine T1/T2 it can be subtle; DWI makes it obvious.

Now a microhaemorrhage on SWI. It's packed with paramagnetic blood-breakdown products that distort the local field, so it blooms dark, appearing far larger than its true size, while staying nearly invisible on conventional sequences. SWI is the sequence for old blood, calcium and small vessels.

Next an enhancing tumour. It breaks the blood-brain barrier, so it takes up contrast. This image is T1 after gadolinium: compared with a plain T1 scan, the tumour brightens, an effect called enhancement, the hallmark of an aggressive or breakdown lesion.

Finally a brain abscess. The case that needs two sequences. On DWI its pus core restricts diffusion and lights up bright (this is how an abscess is told apart from a necrotic tumour, whose core does not restrict).

This is T1 with gadolinium (Spin Echo plus Gadolinium): the abscess shows a thin enhancing rim around the non-enhancing core, the classic 'ring enhancement'. (On T2 the same capsule is a dark ring around the bright pus.) A bright core on DWI and a smooth enhancing rim means abscess. Four lesions, four sequences. That's why an MRI study is never just one scan.

lessons.title: Abscess vs. tumour: the DWI test
lessons.blurb: Two lesions that look identical on contrast, and the one sequence that splits them.

steps.text: Here's a ring-enhancing mass on T1 + gadolinium. The problem: a brain abscess and a necrotic tumour can look identical like this. Both are a bright rim around a dark centre. Yet the treatment is opposite (drain the pus vs. resect/biopsy the tumour), so you have to tell them apart.

DWI splits them. Same lesion on the left and right, now on diffusion. Left. Abscess: the pus restricts diffusion, so the core is bright. Right, necrotic tumour: the core diffuses freely, so it stays dark. That one difference, a bright DWI core. Is what calls it an abscess. (Each panel is labelled with what it is.)

lessons.title: A tour of the real anatomy
lessons.blurb: The same physics on real brain, knee and body atlases.

steps.text: Real brain (BrainWeb), T1-weighted: white matter bright, CSF dark. Each tissue here has its own T1, T2 and PD values driving that contrast.
This is the real knee (a 3-D T2 dataset). A fat-suppressed STIR lights up joint fluid and marrow oedema against nulled fat, the workhorse MSK contrast.
And the real abdomen (TotalSegmentator), T2 FSE: fluid-filled structures bright, solid organs mid-grey. Same equations, real segmented anatomy.

lessons.title: The Ernst angle: flip for max signal
lessons.blurb: On a gradient echo there's an optimal flip, and it isn't 90°.

steps.text: On a gradient echo at short TR, a small flip leaves most of the magnetization unused. Start at 10° and note the WM SNR on the right.
Raise the flip to ~35°, the signal climbs to a peak. This is the Ernst angle: cos α = e−TR/T1, the flip that maximises steady-state signal for a given TR and T1.

Push to 90° and the signal drops. A big flip tips more magnetization but saturates it, at short TR there's no time to recover, so steady-state signal falls. The sweet spot is the Ernst angle, not 90°.

lessons.title: Resolution vs SNR: the matrix trade-off
lessons.blurb: Finer voxels are sharper, but noisier and slower.

steps.text: Baseline: a 256 matrix. Note the resolution, SNR and scan time readouts on the right.
Drop to 96: bigger voxels collect more signal each (higher SNR) over fewer phase-encode lines (faster), but the image is visibly blurrier.
Go to 320: crisp fine detail, but each small voxel holds less signal (lower SNR, grainier) and there are more lines to encode (longer scan). Resolution, SNR and time all pull against each other.

lessons.title: Fat suppression: STIR vs spectral
lessons.blurb: Two ways to darken fat, and why you'd pick each.

steps.text: Real knee, T1 spin echo. fat is bright (subcutaneous fat, marrow). Bright fat can mask oedema and enhancement.
STIR nulls fat by its short T1, inversion recovery at TI ≈ 250 ms. Robust on an uneven field, but it suppresses anything with fat's T1 (not fat-specific) and costs SNR.

Spectral (CHESS) fat-sat instead targets fat's resonant frequency. Fat saturation is on here, on a T2 image. Fat-specific and keeps other short-T1 tissue, but it needs a uniform B0 and fails where the field is distorted.

lessons.title: In- vs opposed-phase (Dixon)
lessons.blurb: Fat and water beating in and out of phase, the India-ink sign.

steps.text: Real abdomen at 1.5 T, gradient echo. At an in-phase TE (4 ms) fat and water in the same voxel add, and the Fat-water phase readout reports In-phase.
Now an opposed-phase TE (2 ms): fat and water point opposite ways and cancel. Voxels with both lose signal, a dark India-ink outline appears at fat-water boundaries (organ edges).
This is the basis of Dixon fat-water imaging and of spotting microscopic fat (adrenal adenoma, fatty liver): tissue that drops signal on opposed- vs in-phase contains intravoxel fat.

lessons.title: Angiography: bright blood (TOF)
lessons.blurb: Flowing blood lights up with no contrast.

steps.text: This is MR Angiography (time-of-flight). Stationary brain is saturated by rapid RF and stays dark, while fresh blood flowing in is unsaturated and bright. Vessels light up with no injection.
At this slice, the bright vessels are inflowing arteries (the circle of Willis). Clinically these are combined into a maximum-intensity projection to show the whole vascular tree at once.

lessons.title: DWI vs ADC: is the restriction real?
lessons.blurb: The ADC map tells true restriction from T2 shine-through.

steps.text: An acute stroke on DWI (high b-value): the infarct restricts water diffusion and lights up bright, the earliest sign of infarction.
But bright on DWI isn't always real restriction. Long-T2 tissue can be bright by T2 shine-through. This is the same case shown as an ADC map.
On the ADC map, genuine restriction is dark (low ADC), the stroke confirms. T2 shine-through would stay bright on ADC. Always read DWI and ADC together.

lessons.title: qMRI: measuring tissue, not a picture
lessons.blurb: Quantitative maps read the actual T1 / T2 in milliseconds.

steps.text: This is Quantitative (qMRI) mode with the T1 map. Instead of a weighted picture, each pixel is the tissue's actual T1 in ms. CSF is long-T1 (bright), white matter short-T1 (dark).

Now the T2 map: each pixel is the actual T2 in ms. These absolute numbers are reproducible across scanners, the basis of quantitative MRI (e.g. cartilage T2, myocardial T1 mapping) where a value, not just contrast, matters.

lessons.title: Reading k-space
lessons.blurb: The raw data the image is the Fourier transform of.

steps.text: This view shows k-space alongside the image. The image isn't acquired pixel-by-pixel. The scanner fills k-space (the spatial-frequency domain), and the image is its 2-D Fourier transform. The bright centre holds low frequencies (contrast and bulk signal).

The edges of k-space hold high spatial frequencies, fine detail and sharp edges. With the matrix dropped to 96, less of k-space's periphery is sampled, so the image blurs (and the readouts show higher SNR, shorter scan).
Back to a full matrix, now with a pulse-sequence diagram shown alongside, connecting the timing, RF, gradients and the echo, to the data each TR writes into k-space.

lessons.title: Parallel imaging & the g-factor
lessons.blurb: Skip k-space lines to go faster. At an SNR cost that isn't uniform.

steps.text: Parallel imaging skips phase-encode lines and unfolds the aliasing using the coil array. Here Acceleration R = 2 is set: the scan time drops, but SNR falls by √R plus a spatially-varying penalty.

This is the g-factor map. The g-factor is that extra, local noise amplification from the unfolding. It is worst toward the centre, where the coil geometry is least able to separate aliased pixels. At R=2 it's mild.

At R = 4, the g-factor map blows up in the centre, since noise amplification grows sharply with R. That's why clinical SENSE rarely exceeds R≈2-3: past that, the g-factor penalty outweighs the time saved.

lessons.title: B0 inhomogeneity & EPI distortion
lessons.blurb: Off-resonance near air-tissue interfaces warps fast sequences.

steps.text: This is the B0 field map. Even after shimming, susceptibility differences (air sinuses, bone) leave the field off-resonance. The map shows the local frequency error in Hz, largest near the skull base and sinuses.

Off-resonance shifts signal along the phase-encode direction in proportion to its size. On a slow spin echo it's negligible, but on EPI (the readout behind DWI/fMRI) the low effective bandwidth makes those same Hz warp and pile up the image. Geometric distortion worst where the field map is most extreme.

lessons.title: Reconstructing the 3D slab (MPR & MIP)
lessons.blurb: One acquisition, reformatted and projected any way you like.

steps.text: This is a 3D slab acquired on a gradient echo with plenty of partitions. The Reconstruction view (under the 3D controls) becomes available once a slab like this exists.

In MPR mode you get the three orthogonal reformats from the one acquisition at once. The crosshair position (Z / A-P / L-R) sets where each reformat cuts through the volume, showing every plane simultaneously, exactly how a workstation navigates a 3D dataset.

This is Thick-slab MIP mode: it keeps the brightest voxel along each ray through an adjustable slab, and a thicker slab pulls bright structures (like vessels) onto a single image. Rotating MIP spins that projection to any angle, and Oblique MPR tilts the reformat plane off the orthogonals.

lessons.title: MIP, MinIP & AIP: projecting a slab
lessons.blurb: Three ways to flatten a slab, and what each is good for.

steps.text: Acquire a 3D slab (gradient echo, plenty of partitions) and open the Reconstruction view, then choose Thick-slab MIP. A projection collapses a slab of partitions onto one image. Three ways, set by the Projection picker.

MIP (maximum) keeps the brightest voxel along each ray, it pulls bright structures onto one image. That's the angiogram trick: bright flowing blood (TOF) stands out, and a thick MIP shows a whole vessel in a single picture.

MinIP (minimum) keeps the darkest voxel. Used where the finding is dark: veins and microbleeds on SWI, or air. AIP (average) is the slab mean, the CT-style look that smooths noise. Same slab, three readings. Pick the one that makes your finding pop.

lessons.title: TOF vs phase-contrast angiography
lessons.blurb: Two ways to make blood bright, inflow vs velocity.

steps.text: Time-of-flight (TOF) MRA: stationary tissue is saturated by rapid RF and dark, while fresh blood flowing in is unsaturated and bright. No contrast, no velocity info, just inflow.

Phase contrast (PC) instead encodes velocity directly: moving spins pick up a phase proportional to their speed (set by the velocity-encoding, venc), so PC measures flow magnitude and direction, useful for quantifying flow, not just showing vessels.

Rule of thumb: TOF for a quick, high-resolution roadmap of where the vessels are (combine slices into a MIP); PC when you need the velocity. Shunts, stenoses, CSF flow. At the cost of a longer, venc-dependent scan.

lessons.title: With contrast: what gadolinium does
lessons.blurb: Why 'post-contrast' scans light up disease, and are always T1.

steps.text: This is a T1 scan with an enhancing tumour painted in. Without contrast it can be subtle, note how it barely stands out from normal brain. (T1: short TR, short TE.)
Now gadolinium has been given. The tumour lights up bright. Gd is a T1-shortening agent. It pools where the blood-brain barrier is broken or tissue is vascular, and short T1 reads bright on T1.

That's the whole idea of 'with contrast': it makes leaky / vascular tissue bright. It only shows on T1-weighted scans, which is why post-contrast series are T1. Comparing the images with and without gadolinium shows the enhancement appear.

lessons.title: Receive coils: why the picture isn't evenly bright
lessons.blurb: The antenna matters: surface coils, arrays and shading.

steps.text: Normally the image looks evenly bright, since the scanner corrects for the receive coil. This is the ideal ('Uniform') coil.

This is a Surface coil. One edge is very bright while the far side fades to dark, since a small loop only 'hears' tissue right next to it. Great local SNR, terrible coverage. This is why spine and joint surface coils sit against the body part.

Now a Head array (8-ch): it covers the whole head, but its raw sensitivity still varies (brighter near the elements). That residual shading is exactly what the scanner's intensity correction flattens to give the clean image you started with.

lessons.title: Balanced SSFP: bright fluid, fast
lessons.blurb: The speed sequence: T2/T1 contrast and its banding artifact.

steps.text: Balanced SSFP (TrueFISP / FIESTA / bSSFP) is very fast and gives bright fluid, its contrast follows T2/T1, so fluid and vessels glow regardless of TE. Used for cardiac cine, fetal and MRCP-type imaging where speed matters.
Because the signal is refocused every TR, it's SNR-efficient and tolerates short TRs. That's where the speed comes from. The trade-off is on the next step.

bSSFP's weakness is off-resonance banding. Dark stripes where the field is uneven (near air/metal, at high field). The bands sit at Δf = ±1/2·TR, so keeping TR short pushes them out of the anatomy. It's the price of all that speed and signal.

lessons.title: SWI: veins, iron & old blood
lessons.blurb: Long-TE gradient echo that 'blooms' anything magnetic.

steps.text: Susceptibility-weighted imaging is a long-TE gradient echo tuned to anything that distorts the local magnetic field, deoxygenated venous blood, iron, calcium, old haemorrhage. Veins appear dark.

Add a microhaemorrhage (Pathology → microhaemorrhage). On SWI it 'blooms' into a dark spot much larger than the actual bleed, the field disturbance spreads beyond the iron itself. That sensitivity is the whole point.

SWI combines the GRE magnitude with a phase mask, and a minimum-intensity projection turns the veins into a venogram. It's the go-to for trauma (diffuse axonal injury), cavernomas, and counting microbleeds.

lessons.title: fMRI: watching the brain light up
lessons.blurb: BOLD: function as a statistical map, not one picture.

steps.text: fMRI uses fast T2*-weighted EPI to watch blood oxygenation change as the brain works (the BOLD effect). This is the raw EPI image, low-res and a bit distorted, but acquired many times per second.
This is the Activation Map. Colour marks where signal rose during a task, a tiny (~1-3%) change, teased out of a long time series and overlaid on the anatomy.

The T-statistic map is the honest version: it shows how confident we are that each voxel truly responded, not merely that it changed. The lesson: fMRI is statistics on a time series, not a single snapshot. Which is why it needs a task design and careful thresholding.

lessons.title: Slice thickness & partial volume
lessons.blurb: Thick = bright but blurry, thin = sharp but noisy.

steps.text: Slice thickness sets how thick a slab of tissue each pixel represents. Start thin (2 mm): small structures stay sharp and distinct, but each pixel collects signal from less tissue, so it's noisier (lower SNR). (Slice thickness is in the Acquisition section.)

Now go thick (10 mm). The image gets visibly brighter / cleaner, SNR rises because each pixel averages more tissue. The cost: small structures blur, their signal smeared together with neighbours. That averaging across a thick slab is partial-volume effect.

The Partial volume control exaggerates that sub-voxel mixing so you can see it directly, boundaries soften as it rises. The trade is always the same: thin for small lesions and fine anatomy (accept the noise), thick for a quick survey or low-SNR sequences. There's no free lunch. Only the right pick for the question.

lessons.title: Bandwidth: the hidden three-way trade
lessons.blurb: Receiver bandwidth balances SNR, chemical shift and speed.

steps.text: Receiver bandwidth is how fast the scanner samples each echo, a setting people forget, but it trades off three things at once: SNR, chemical-shift artifact, and readout speed. Chemical shift is turned on here so it's visible. This is a middle bandwidth (125 kHz).

This is a lower bandwidth (≈32 kHz). SNR rises (it scales as 1/√BW. Narrow bandwidth hears less noise), but the fat/water chemical-shift misregistration gets worse: fat shifts further along the readout direction, smearing organ edges. Low BW buys signal but pays in chemical shift (and a longer echo).

This is a higher bandwidth (≈400 kHz). Chemical shift shrinks to almost nothing and the readout is fast (shorter echo train, less blur and less EPI distortion), at the cost of SNR. So: high BW for EPI / diffusion and around metal; low BW when you need every drop of signal and fat shift doesn't matter. Bandwidth is the quiet knob that ties SNR, artifact and speed together.

lessons.title: Choosing the protocol (capstone)
lessons.blurb: Put it together: question → sequence, plane and options.

steps.text: Everything so far feeds one decision: what answers the clinical question? Work it as sequence → plane → options. Example, ?acute stroke: diffusion restricts early, so DWI (with the ADC map) is the answer, shown here.
?MS lesion load: small periventricular lesions hide in bright CSF, so null the CSF. FLAIR, read in the plane that shows the most lesions. Long TR, long TE, TI≈2550 ms at 3 T.

?Vascular anatomy: flowing blood, no contrast. TOF MRA, then a thick-slab MIP to show the whole tree. The pattern is always the same: name the contrast that makes the finding obvious, pick the plane that shows it, then add the options (fat-sat, Gd, 3D, projection) that sharpen it.

lessons.title: Planning the scan: coverage, angle & the queue
lessons.blurb: Prescribe each scan on the localizer, then build a whole study.

steps.text: Real scans aren't acquired blind. Each is prescribed on a quick localizer first. With FOV planning shown, the cross panels display a scout, and a coloured box marks where this scan's slices sit, their position, coverage and angle. Right now it's a single slice through the middle of the head.

Coverage. One slice won't cover an organ, so you prescribe a stack. Here 20 slices are set: the bands fill the brain on the cross panels, and the scan time climbs on the right. More coverage costs time, and that's the first planning trade.

Angle. Heads (and joints, and spines) are rarely straight, so the stack is tilted to line it up with the anatomy, angling the axial slices along the skull base, or to match a tilted head. An oblique prescription is the difference between a symmetric, readable study and a wonky one. The acquired image comes out in the plane that was set.

A real study is many such scans. Each prescribed, then acquired in turn. That's what the dedicated Protocol Planning workspace is for: in the browser open it from the toolbar link; on the desktop it's the Protocol panel on the left. Pick an exam (Brain, Spine or Knee), a queue of sequences loads, and you prescribe each on the three scouts and hit Acquire. Scan time and SNR are tallied as the series builds. Same prescription skills you just used, end to end.

lessons.title: Perfusion: blood flow, stroke and tumour grade
lessons.blurb: Map blood flow without a needle (ASL), then with a contrast bolus (DSC/DCE), and read a stroke against a tumour.

steps.text: Perfusion imaging maps blood flow, not just anatomy. The simplest is arterial spin labeling (ASL): it magnetically tags arterial blood as a tracer, so it needs no contrast injection. This is the quantitative CBF map (cerebral blood flow, mL/100 g/min): grey matter is bright (~60), white matter dark (~22): cortex is perfused 2-3× more than white matter. The curve below shows the tagged signal fading as the post-label delay grows (the label decays with blood's T1).

The workhorse is DSC (dynamic susceptibility contrast): a gadolinium bolus is tracked as it passes through the brain. The curve below is that first pass; the area under it is the blood volume (CBV), the width is the mean transit time (MTT), and the peak follows flow. This is the CBV map; like CBF, grey > white.

This is a stroke. The infarct core has lost its supply, so on the CBF map it is a dark hole of reduced flow against the cortex. On the MTT map that same territory is prolonged: the blood that does arrive transits slowly. Low CBF with long MTT is the signature of the ischaemic core. The labels here help locate it; the infarct's bolus curve below is the low, delayed one.

This is a tumour on CBV: the mass is bright. It has grown its own vessels (neovascularisation), so its blood volume is raised, and high CBV means a high-grade tumour. This is how perfusion grades a mass that can look bland on routine images. Its bolus curve below is the tall one.

This is Ktrans (DCE), a T1 acquisition that measures how fast contrast leaks across the blood-brain barrier. Normal brain keeps the barrier shut, so it stays dark (Ktrans ≈ 0); the tumour's leaky vessels light up. The curve makes it plain: normal tissue stays flat while the tumour enhances over time. ASL flow, DSC volume and transit, DCE permeability: three views of perfusion that together separate a stroke from a tumour.

lessons.title: MR safety: fields, zones & screening
lessons.blurb: Why the magnet is always dangerous: the four zones, the projectile effect, screening, and the gradient/RF/quench hazards.

steps.text: MRI uses no ionising radiation, but the magnet is always on, even between patients, so safety is built around three ever-present fields: the strong static field, the switching gradients, and the RF pulses. Facilities are split into four zones of rising control: Zone I is freely public; Zone IV is the scanner room itself, entered only under the direct supervision of trained MR personnel.

The static field's biggest danger is the projectile (‘missile’) effect: it pulls ferromagnetic (iron-containing) objects toward the bore with lethal force: an oxygen cylinder, an IV pole, even scissors. Nothing ferromagnetic enters Zone IV. Equipment is labelled MR-safe (no metal), MR-conditional (safe under stated conditions), or MR-unsafe.

Everyone and everything is screened before entering. Implants are the crux: a ferromagnetic aneurysm clip can move, a conductive wire can heat, and an active device such as a pacemaker can malfunction. Each implant is checked against its MR-conditional labelling. When in doubt, keep it out.

The other two fields have their own limits. Rapidly switching gradients (high dB/dt) can cause peripheral nerve stimulation (tingling or muscle twitching), so the scanner caps dB/dt. The RF pulses deposit energy as heat, measured by the SAR (W/kg); high SAR risks burns, so avoid looped cables and skin-to-skin contact, and the scanner limits SAR.

Finally, the emergency: a quench. The superconducting magnet suddenly goes resistive and boils off its liquid helium, which should vent outside through the quench pipe. If venting fails, the cold gas can displace room oxygen (an asphyxiation risk), so know the oxygen-monitor alarm and the evacuation route.

lessons.title: Patient care: screening, contrast & monitoring
lessons.blurb: The patient journey: screening, preparation, positioning, contrast safety and monitoring.

steps.text: MRI safety starts with screening. Every patient completes a detailed questionnaire before every scan: status changes, and new implants or devices may have appeared since a prior study. Screen for pacemakers, aneurysm clips, cochlear implants, neurostimulators and any metal. A grinder or metalworker with possible intra-orbital metal needs orbital radiographs first.

Prepare the patient. Remove all ferromagnetic items: jewellery, hairpins, watches, cards, hearing aids, clothing with metal. Explain the exam and its loud knocking noise, and provide hearing protection: gradient switching reaches ~100-120 dB and can damage hearing. Confirm the questionnaire one more time before entering Zone IV.

Position for signal and comfort. Centre the target anatomy in the coil and at isocentre for the best signal and field homogeneity, and immobilise gently to minimise motion; a still, relaxed patient gives the best images. Hand over the call button / squeeze-ball and explain how to reach you at any time.

If gadolinium is used, screen renal function (eGFR): severe impairment risks nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. Also ask about prior contrast reactions. Watch for acute reactions (hives, wheeze, low blood pressure); know the emergency plan and where drugs and oxygen are kept. In pregnancy, gadolinium is avoided unless essential.

Monitor the patient throughout. Keep verbal contact between sequences and watch for distress or claustrophobia: reassure, use the call system, take a break, and consider a wide/open-bore magnet or sedation. Sedated or unstable patients need physiological monitoring with MR-safe equipment only.
